confirmed: Source: the complete on-file markdown was read through the final Figure List, including references and the repeated figures on pp. 28-31. The PDF has 31 pages; its title and five authors match the form. The retrieval record identifies arXiv 2606.27067; the manuscript has no printed revision identifier or publication date. No separate appendix or supplement is identified (PDF p. 1 and pp. 24-31; retrieval.json, c307).

Randomized people study confirmed: children were randomly assigned to the two counterbalanced condition orders, and each child used StoryPrompt and a traditional storyboard. Retain lab_rct for these individually facilitated, supervised sessions in school classrooms; reanalysis of the dataset does not make the study observational or a synthesis (PDF p. 9, Section 3.3; p. 10, Figures 2-3; p. 11, Section 3.5).

The sample comprised 40 children, 30 boys and 10 girls, aged 7-12 in Grades 2-6. P36 and P39 lacked completed storyboard stories and were excluded from every quantitative analysis, leaving 38 children; their AI-condition observations/interviews remained in qualitative analyses. These counts are people, not stories or ratings (PDF p. 9, Section 3.2).

The 38 analyzed children are the same people in both conditions. N = 18 AI-first and N = 20 traditional-first describe the analyzed order groups. Assignment-stage group counts are not separately reported, so the form appropriately leaves n_randomized null rather than treating these complete-case counts as randomized counts (PDF p. 9, Sections 3.2-3.3; p. 12, order-specific robustness analyses).

Eligibility is correctly core = no, criterion 1 = met, criterion 2 = not_met, criterion 3 = met, context_class = none: 38 analyzed people is below 50, but random condition order and expert-scored creative output require the randomized-people screening route (PDF pp. 9-10, Sections 3.2-3.4; codebook Sections 3-4).

StoryPrompt used GPT-3.5 for eight keyword options per paragraph, four strongly and four weakly associated, and Stable Diffusion for images. Children composed six paragraphs across three scenes and authored the narrative prose themselves, in Chinese. The AI task took 20-30 minutes; Figure 2 specifies a maximum of 30 minutes per condition (PDF pp. 8-10, Sections 3.1-3.4 and Figure 2; p. 13, Section 4.1).

S1-O1 numbers match: bottom-tercile creativity gain +1.292 with N = 13; top-tercile overall composite gain −0.292 with N = 13; descriptive creativity variance ratio 2.27×. The −0.292 is explicitly an overall-quality gain, not a creativity gain. Figure 4 has no exact numeric label for the top-tercile creativity bar (PDF p. 12, Section 4.1 and Figure 4; p. 14, Section 4.1).

S1-O2 numbers match: 27 of 38 children had positive composite-quality gains and 11 had negative gains. The order comparison is AI-first N = 18, M = 0.21, SD = 0.80 versus traditional-first N = 20, M = 0.32, SD = 0.52; Mann-Whitney U = 185.5, p = .884. This test compares gains between order groups (PDF p. 9, Section 3.3; p. 11, Section 4.1).

The median-split composite-quality gap decreased by 83.5%, from 1.028 traditional-condition points to 0.170 AI-condition points. The authors call this descriptive score compression and explicitly reject interpreting it as an independent causal estimate (PDF p. 14, Section 4.1 and Figure 7).

S1-O3 numbers match: bottom-tercile richness gain +1.369 with N = 13; lower-grade versus higher-grade richness M = 3.547 versus 3.600, p = .883 under AI, and M = 2.726 versus 3.205, p = .086 under traditional storyboarding. Those p-values compare grade groups within conditions (PDF pp. 12-13, Section 4.1).

The one-line finding correctly reports baseline-gain Spearman rs = −0.730, p < .001, bottom-tercile creativity gain +1.292, 38 analyzed children, and the 83.5% gap reduction from 1.028 to 0.170. Aggregate AI-versus-storyboard means are not numerically printed for the three recorded outcomes; subgroup means/gains and graphical distributions are provided (PDF pp. 11-14, Section 4.1 and Figures 4-7).

The convergence result concerns quality-score compression, not measured similarity or diversity of story content. There is no after-AI creative-output assessment and no pooled synthesis estimate to extract (PDF p. 23, Section 5.4; p. 24, Limitations and Conclusion).

Source count discrepancy: Figure 2 labels higher-grade children n = 8, whereas Section 3.2 reports the higher-grade group N = 18 and lower-grade group N = 22. This figure inconsistency does not change the explicitly stated total of 40 participants and 38 quantitative cases (PDF p. 9, Section 3.2; p. 10, Figure 2, repeated on p. 28).

No company involvement is disclosed: the listed funding is from Chinese public research funds, and the authors declare no relevant financial or non-financial interests (PDF p. 24, Acknowledgements; p. 25, Declarations of interest statement).
summary: This paper reanalyzes a randomized-order storytelling experiment with 38 children analyzed, so it requires randomized-people screening but falls below the 50-person core threshold. The recorded numerical results match the PDF; corrections add omitted outcomes, measurement and statistics details, the shared-sample record, and the dataset link.
